d.title: Twenty-one milliseconds, and one request in a hundred took 26.84
d.caption: **Reporting “about 21 ms” hides the shape: P99 is 1.25× the median even on an idle machine with four threads and nothing else running.** On a loaded server — garbage collection, thread contention, noisy neighbours — that tail stretches much further. **Which is why SLOs are written against P95 or P99: it is what users actually experience, and a service whose mean is fine and whose tail is not will read as “sometimes slow” rather than as a latency problem.**

steps.note: and this is an idle machine

d.title: The knee is at 16, and 32 was marginally worse
d.caption: Per-item cost falls from **21.958 ms to 7.586 ms — a 2.9× throughput gain — and then flattens.** Past 16 there is essentially nothing left: **32 was marginally *worse* and 64 gained under 1%.** So **the knee is the batch size to ship, because everything past it adds queueing latency for no throughput** — a batch of 64 makes the first request in the batch wait 480 ms to be served at the same per-item rate as a batch of 16.

d.title: One long document made the batch 39 times slower
d.caption: Thirty-two documents, `padding=True`: **all short pads to (32, 3) at 58.91 ms, and 31 short plus one long pads to (32, 158) at 2319.61 ms.** The 31 short documents are now 155 columns of padding each, **so the cost of a batch is set by its longest member and nothing else.** Which is why **`padding="max_length"` is usually wrong in training — it pads everything to the model maximum regardless of content** — and why `DataCollatorWithPadding` plus a length-grouped sampler is the standard setup.

state: the longest member sets the cost

d.title: 1.79x faster, 48% smaller, and the logits moved by 0.0238
d.caption: int8 dynamic quantisation on CPU: **23.81 ms to 13.29 ms, 267.9 MB to 138.7 MB, and the second logit shifted from 0.0397 to 0.0635.** A max absolute difference of **0.0238** is usually harmless and is not nothing — **it is enough to flip a prediction sitting near a decision threshold, which is exactly the population a calibrated classifier cares about.** The other routes compose with this one: **ONNX Runtime for 2–5× through operator fusion, and distillation from 340M down to 14M.**

steps.note: enough to flip a borderline case

d.title: Four lines of code absorbed 81.6% of the traffic
d.caption: **Real query traffic is not uniform — it is heavily skewed, with a small number of queries accounting for most requests — which makes caching the cheapest optimisation available and the one most often skipped.** A 1,024-entry `lru_cache` over 2,000 requests across 500 distinct queries: **1,632 hits, 81.6% hit rate, 6.78s against approximately 36.86s — a 5.4× cut in wall-clock with no model change and no hardware.** In a real service: Redis so it survives restarts and is shared across replicas, keyed on the **normalised** input.

d.title: The bug was invisible until someone swapped the checkpoint
d.caption: The probe is `"EXCELLENT Service"`, and on `bert-base-uncased` **both paths agree — because the tokenizer lowercases anyway, so a serving path that forgets to lowercase is indistinguishable from one that does.** Then the checkpoint changes to `bert-base-cased` and **the serve path produces `['E', '##X', '##CE', '##LL', '##EN', '##T', 'Service']`: seven subword tokens where training produced two words.** Accuracy degrades, **and every test still passes, because both paths work perfectly in isolation.**

d.title: Four stages, and the last row is the one that changes the cost model
d.caption: Most of this is the lesson's own measurements turned into instructions — **benchmark after warm-up, enforce a max input length, bucket by length, and track percentiles rather than means.** The scaling row has the item worth noticing: **a cascade, where a cheap model runs first and the expensive one runs only when it abstains**, which turns the P99 problem into a routing problem. And **logging the prediction distribution is what catches drift**, because accuracy needs labels and the distribution does not.

d.title: One row per word type, which no amount of training data fixes
d.caption: **A static embedding is a lookup table: Word2Vec, GloVe and fastText all produce one row per word type — so a word with several meanings gets one vector, which must be some average of its senses, and no downstream model can recover the distinction because the information was never there.** And 3.2 made the scale concrete from WordNet: **`bank` has 18 senses and `run` has 57. Those are not edge cases — polysemy is the normal condition of frequent words.**

nodes.label: So one vector averages every sense
The information is not lost - never present
And more data does not help
Polysemy is normal for frequent words

d.title: Same-sense pairs score higher than cross-sense pairs, and a static embedding scores 1.0 for all four
d.caption: Four sentences, two senses of `bank`, BERT's final layer. **Same-sense pairs sit at 0.5065 and 0.4023; cross-sense pairs at 0.2789 and 0.2736** — a clear separation, and worth noting that even the same-sense pairs are nowhere near 1.0, because the contexts still differ. **The comparison row is the finding: a static embedding returns 1.0000 for every row by construction**, so it does not score this problem badly — it cannot represent the question.

d.title: Separation peaks at layer 4, not at the top
d.caption: **Layer 0 separates the two senses by exactly +0.0000 — the embedding layer is the lookup table, so there is nothing to separate. Separation rises to +0.2867 at layer 4 and then declines to +0.1782 at layer 12.** So the final layer is **not** the most sense-discriminative one, which is §07's practical consequence. And the direct confirmation of the mechanism: **comparing layer-0 vectors for `bank` across two sentences gives 0.971274 rather than 1.0, and the only reason is the positional embedding.**

d.title: Five words, all entering indistinguishable and leaving separated
d.caption: The pattern holds for every word tested: **layer 0 between 0.9575 and 1.0000, layer 12 between 0.2789 and 0.5831.** `light` is the clean case — **it starts at a perfect 1.0000 because it occupies the same position in both probe sentences, so even the positional embedding matches — and ends at 0.4073.** Which isolates the mechanism exactly: **nothing about the input differed, and twelve layers of attention reading the surrounding words produced the whole gap.**

d.title: The semantic contrast separates and the syntactic one comes back together
d.caption: Two probes through the depth: **the same sense in two grammatical roles, against two different senses.** The semantic contrast falls monotonically — 0.9713 to 0.2789 — while **the syntactic contrast bottoms out at 0.8283 by layer 8 and then rises to 0.8740 at layer 12.** So the upper layers are **re-converging** on grammatical role while still separating meaning, which is the measured version of the probing literature's claim that **syntax is concentrated below semantics.**

d.title: Five cases, and the first one removes the question
d.caption: **If you can afford to fine-tune the whole model, the question does not arise — gradients update every layer — and that is the preference.** For frozen features the measurements above give the answer: **middle layers, roughly 4–8, because sense separation peaked at 4 and was still strong through 8**, and lower-middle for a syntactic task. Two warnings: **mean-pooling the final layer is a weak sentence encoder**, and when unsure, **concatenate or learn a weighted sum — ELMo's original answer, and still the safe default.**

items.sub: NOT the final layer alone - use sentence-transformers

d.title: Three members of one chain, found by three different detectors
d.caption: **`Barack Obama` came from NER, `He` from the POS tagger, and `The former senator` from noun chunking** — so **mention detection is already a union of several detectors, each with its own errors**, before any linking happens. And the four mention types differ in difficulty in a specific way: **pronouns are trivially detected and hard to resolve; nominal phrases need the system to know the description fits the entity; demonstratives often refer to events or whole propositions rather than entities.**

d.title: The relation extractor produced a fact whose subject is a pronoun
d.caption: Two sentences, and the output is **`('It', 'cost', '$999')`** — syntactically correct and useless, because `It` is not a node in any knowledge graph. **The entity list shows why nothing can repair it downstream: `Apple` and `999` were found, and nothing connects the pronoun to either.** Which is the argument for coreference as a pipeline stage rather than a research topic: **extraction over multi-sentence text produces dangling subjects by default.**

d.title: One word changes what the pronoun refers to, and the parse is identical
d.caption: **Same parse, same entities, same pronoun position — swapping *big* for *small* changes what *it* refers to, and nothing in the grammar records that.** Resolving them requires knowing **that a container must be larger than the thing it contains**, which is world knowledge rather than syntax. This is the Winograd schema shape, and it is the reason coreference resisted rule-based approaches for decades: **the signal is not in the sentence.**

steps.code: '...doesn't fit in the suitcase because it is too big.'
'...doesn't fit in the suitcase because it is too small.'

d.title: Two of seven right, and the five failures are five different failures
d.caption: The two active-voice sentences with a single clause work. **Then: a copular sentence returns nothing, a passive returns nothing, coordination merges two facts into one malformed triple, apposition returns a correct span that is a useless key, and a negated sentence emits the relation as if it were asserted.** Note the last one specifically — **`Google did not acquire Yahoo` produces `('Google', 'acquire', 'Yahoo')`**, which is not a miss but a **false fact**, and the only one of the five that corrupts data rather than losing it.

d.title: Five failures, five one-line causes in the parse
d.caption: Each failure traces to a single feature of the dependency tree. **In the passive, `Google` hangs off the preposition *by* as `pobj`, not off the verb — so it is never considered.** The copular root is `is`, tagged `AUX` not `VERB`, **so a `pos_ == "VERB"` guard rejects the sentence before anything else runs.** And only one token per sentence is `ROOT`, **so a second clause's verb is `conj` and its entire relation is silently dropped.** Fixing each means a rule per construction, **which is the moment a rule-based extractor stops being cheaper than a model.**

the appositive is in the span
its verb is conj, not ROOT

d.title: Three classes, and the third is the one that matters in practice
d.caption: **Entailment is not “consistent with” — it is *forced by*. Contradiction is active incompatibility. And neutral is the class that matters most in practice: consistent with the premise but not supported by it.** The measured row makes it concrete: *“The man is a professional musician”* given *“A man is playing a guitar on stage”* is **NEUTRAL at 0.997** — plausible, unsupported, and exactly the kind of sentence a summariser invents. **MNLI's genre diversity is why MNLI-trained models transfer better than SNLI's image captions.**

steps.code: guitar on stage -> sleeping at home
guitar on stage -> a professional musician
two dogs in a field -> animals outdoors

d.title: The wall 2.6 and 3.4 both hit, and the metric that gets over it
d.caption: **ROUGE and BERTScore cannot see a hallucinated fact. NLI can** — treat the source as the premise and each generated sentence as a hypothesis. Three faithful sentences come back ENTAILMENT at 0.977–0.993, a reversed figure comes back **CONTRADICTION at 0.989**, and an invented forecast comes back **NEUTRAL** — which is the right verdict for an unsupported claim rather than a false one. **The production shape is a pipeline stage: split, check each sentence, route anything not entailed to a human or drop it — one forward pass per sentence, cheap next to the generation.**

d.title: There is no zero-shot model — there is an NLI model and a template
d.caption: **`facebook/bart-large-mnli` is an NLI model. The zero-shot pipeline loops over candidate labels, builds a hypothesis from a template, and normalises the entailment probabilities** — that is the entire mechanism, written out. Which tells you how to improve it, and it is not the model: **the hypothesis template is a prompt.** *“This example is about travel”* scores 0.9438, and a template matching how your labels are actually phrased will score differently on the same text.

nodes.label: So the template is a prompt
Not the model
nodes.sub: which is where people tune first

d.title: Synonym replacement produced “The Robert William Service at this restaurant”
d.caption: **The premise is that a label-preserving transformation produces a valid new example, and the whole difficulty is whether it actually does.** Here is what WordNet synonym replacement produced: **`service` became the proper noun `Robert William Service`, `product` became `Cartesian product`, and `terrible` became `dead abominable`.** The first four EDA methods are **easy in exactly the way that hides the problem** — senses and proper nouns leak in, and the output is training data the model then learns from.

steps.code: 'The service at this restaurant was excellent'

d.title: Five tasks, and what is unsafe is decided by where the label lives
d.caption: The rule behind every row: **ask what the label is attached to.** Topic is carried redundantly across many words, so deletion is fine. **Sentiment often rests on one word — delete *terrible* and the label is now wrong.** NER's label **is** the span offsets, so any reordering invalidates every annotation. **And for NLI the label is the relation between two sentences, so changing the hypothesis changes the label by definition.** QA is the same shape: the answer is a span with character offsets into the context.
